slides.text: Julian Thorne never made mistakes. At the conservatory, he was a piano prodigy carved from ice, renowned for his flawless, soulless precision. I was his opposite: messy, emotional, and eternally trapped in second place behind his shadow. We hated each other with the burning passion of true rivals. For our final showcase, the cruel faculty forced us into a duet. Rehearsals were warzones. I played to break his walls; he played to show me they were impenetrable.

The night of the showcase, the auditorium was packed. We sat at the grand piano, our shoulders inches apart. The piece was impossibly fast, a dizzying waltz of overlapping hands. I poured all my frustration into the keys, daring him to keep up. He met my fury, matching my tempo perfectly, his face a mask of cold concentration. We were hurtling toward the terrifying crescendo, the moment he always used to obliterate my performance with his mechanical perfection.

Then, the impossible happened. Just as the spotlight flared for the final sequence, Julian’s finger slipped. A glaring, dissonant chord echoed through the hall. The audience gasped. Instinct took over, and I seamlessly covered his error, soaring into a breathtaking, improvised solo that brought the crowd to its feet. Amidst the deafening applause, I turned to Julian, furious. But he wasn't upset. He was smiling at me, his icy eyes completely melted. 'You deserved to shine,' he whispered.
